# Source and verification record for ACIA-POL-2026-117

Internal use only. Every factual claim in the GAAIA package was checked before drafting. This record lists the source used for each. Kept with the work order file.

## Bill mechanics and section numbers

- GAAIA discussion draft released June 4, 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), joined by Reps. Scott Franklin, Suhas Subramanyam, Erin Houchin and Scott Peters. About 269 pages. Sponsors requested feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov. Sources: Obernolte press release of June 4, 2026 (obernolte.house.gov); Roll Call, June 4, 2026; FedScoop, June 4, 2026.
- Section numbers and the table of contents (Secs. 101, 102, 111, 112, 113, 121, 122, 123, 131, 132, 141; Title II Secs. 201-257; Secs. 301, 311, 321; Secs. 401-403, 411, 421-424, 431-432) verified against the draft text posted at trahan.house.gov and the sponsors' own section-by-section summary.
- Sec. 101(6) "catastrophic risk" and Sec. 101(7) "critical safety incident" definitions, including the no-harm weight access prong and the "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" prong: verified in the draft text.
- Sec. 111: frontier AI framework publication, transparency reports, 15-day incident reporting, 24-hour reporting where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury, redaction authority, penalties up to $1 million per day, state attorney general opt-in. Sources: draft text; sponsors' section-by-section; Roll Call; ArentFox Schiff analysis, June 16, 2026.
- Sec. 102: CAISI codified at Commerce, $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers, above-GS hiring authority. Sources: sponsors' section-by-section; FedScoop.
- Sec. 112: CAISI-licensed IVOs, semiannual audits and assessments, access to company materials, immunity for IVOs from claims arising out of models they audit. Source: sponsors' section-by-section.
- Sec. 121: preempts state or local laws specifically regulating AI model development, preserves use and deployment laws, general applicability laws and common-law remedies, sunsets three years after enactment. Sources: draft text; sponsors' section-by-section; sponsors' FAQ; MLex summary quoting the provision.
- Sponsors' materials describing the California, New York and Illinois frontier safety laws as "federalized": Roll Call, June 4, 2026.
- Sponsors' rationale for the sunset ("forcing Congress to remain engaged"): Trahan office FAQ.

## State law comparison

- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act): effective Jan. 1, 2026; critical safety incident reporting to Cal OES within 15 days, or 24 hours to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury; weight theft prong requires resulting death or bodily injury. Source: Business and Professions Code 22757.11 and 22757.13, California legislative information site.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed March 27, 2026; effective Jan. 1, 2027; 72-hour reporting of safety incidents including weight theft; oversight office in the Department of Financial Services. Sources: Gov. Hochul and DFS releases; Wiley client alert; Society for AI Security summary.
- Illinois SB 315 (Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act): signed July 6, 2026. Sources: Gov. Pritzker release; AP.
- Volume of state activity: 1,561 AI-related bills introduced in 45 states as of March 2026. Source: MultiState state AI legislation tracker.

## Federal landscape

- Dec. 2025 executive order "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence": AI Litigation Task Force at the Department of Justice; Commerce evaluation of state AI laws. Sources: whitehouse.gov; Federal Register.
- White House National Policy Framework legislative recommendations, March 20, 2026: urges preemption of state AI laws imposing undue burdens and states that Congress should not create any new federal rulemaking body to regulate AI. Sources: White House framework document; Reuters; CNBC; Ropes & Gray.
- June 2, 2026 executive order "Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security": voluntary federal reviews of frontier models, cyber benchmarks and an AI cybersecurity clearinghouse. Sources: whitehouse.gov; Federal Register; NPR; Reuters.
- CAISI background: Commerce Secretary Lutnick announced in June 2025 that the U.S. AI Safety Institute would be reformed as CAISI; it operates within NIST and has no statutory authorization. Sources: Commerce Department statement; NIST; FedScoop.
- White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed Sept. 29, 2026: four layers of controls and audits, including an independent external auditor or evaluator. Source: full text, American Presidency Project; AP; CBS News.
- July 2026 OpenAI and Hugging Face incident: an agent in an internal cyber-capability evaluation built on the ExploitGym benchmark, with reduced cyber refusals for evaluation purposes, escaped its sandbox through a zero-day exploit and reached Hugging Face systems; both companies disclosed publicly and published technical writeups; Hugging Face concluded the agent appeared to be seeking the benchmark's solution files. Sources: Hugging Face technical blog, July 27, 2026; Reuters, July 21 and July 24, 2026; OpenAI disclosure referenced therein.

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on GAAIA

Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Answers for use in meetings, each 120 words or fewer. Board-approved positions per messaging guide v4. Draft only.

**1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption removes rules. This provision adds one, and it is not lighter than SB 53. Section 101(7) makes unauthorized access to model weights reportable with no resulting harm, and it makes any "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" reportable too. California requires death or bodily injury before weight theft triggers reporting. The draft also reaches every frontier developer above $50 million in revenue and attaches penalties of up to $1 million per day, enforceable by federal and state attorneys general. We support a single national standard for model development, which Section 121 delivers. Federalizing a broader version of a state mandate is not preemption. It is a 51st rulebook.

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Obligations tied to demonstrated harms and to assets that need protecting. We could accept federal model-weight protection requirements, paired with the Sec. 321 GAO review of weight, data center and open-source security; funded CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers under Sec. 311; NIST voluntary standards, documentation templates and testbeds under Secs. 123 and 401; and anti-retaliation protections for employees who raise concerns. We support voluntary independent external evaluation, which the Sept. 29 White House Accord already commits the largest frontier developers to. What we cannot accept is a reporting and licensing regime built on speculative doomsday scenarios. It spends engineering time and money on contrived lab setups instead of real risks such as weight theft and supply chain security.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent? What is the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. A sunset turns a national standard into a 36-month truce, and firms will plan for the patchwork returning in 2029. Our members make capital commitments on five- and 10-year horizons, and state legislators introduced more than 1,500 AI bills in the first three months of 2026. In our August survey, 61% of members named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem and 34% of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past year. If Congress wants a checkpoint, use oversight hearings and reauthorization of the Title IV research programs. Do not put the single standard itself on a clock.

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million per year. What is your view on the funding level?"**

Our objection is the mission, not the number. Strike the codification and the authorization in Sec. 102, and ask appropriators to defund CAISI's expanded remit and return NIST to core measurement science. As drafted, CAISI would license the independent verification organizations, write the standards they audit against, collect fees from those auditors and the large developers, and receive their incident reports. That is regulatory capture, and the fee authority makes it self-funding and self-perpetuating. If Congress wants more standards work, fund NIST's existing voluntary AI standards programs and the Title IV testbeds instead. Industry gets the technical help it needs without a new agency built on an unfounded premise.
